data.description:
## Discovered from

rebar-debug on bug `smart-disloyal-naga` (8386-a512-4815-4e6b). Re-verified there by two
methods and by runtime observation; recorded rather than fixed, because removing it is a
public-dataclass change unrelated to that bug's performance fix.

## Problem

`SnapshotHandle._cleanup` (`src/rebar/_snapshot/repo_snapshot.py:199`) is declared as
`Callable[[], None] | None = None` and read only by `__exit__` (`:212-213`). **No producer
anywhere in `src/` ever assigns it.** `grep -rn "_cleanup" src/` returns exactly those two
sites; Serena agrees.

Confirmed at runtime through a real `resolve_gate_handle(...)`:

    handle.source=attested sha=49d6fb2e tickets_path=set
    handle._cleanup = None
    after __exit__: cleanup invoked? False  (entry still on disk: True)

So `SnapshotHandle.__exit__` is a permanent no-op, and `with handle:` reads — to anyone
skimming — as though it releases something.

## Why it matters

It is not a leak (the entry is a *cache*; per-review release would defeat caching, which is why
8386 was fixed by adding reuse rather than by adding release). The cost is that it is
**misleading dead code** on a class whose whole subject is resource lifetime, in the exact
module where a reader goes to ask "who cleans these up?". The honest answer is "the janitor,
never the handle", and the field says otherwise.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Either the field is removed (and `__enter__`/`__exit__` kept or dropped deliberately), or
      it is assigned by a real producer with a documented purpose.
- [ ] If removed, `SnapshotHandle`'s docstring states that entry lifetime is the janitor's
      responsibility and not the handle's.
- [ ] No caller constructs `SnapshotHandle(_cleanup=...)` (verified: none does today).
data.title: Remove or wire SnapshotHandle._cleanup — no producer assigns it, so __exit__ is a no-op
